metadata.title: Teachers’ emotional exhaustion and job satisfaction: How much does the school context matter?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses two German teacher survey datasets (DiScH and SchuMaS) with teachers clustered within schools, and the authors explicitly model this hierarchical structure using multilevel regression with random intercepts. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights (e.g., student-level design weights) or any replicate-weight scheme; therefore, no weight variable is specified. Missing data are handled via full information maximum likelihood (FIML), which is implemented in the modeling stage rather than through weight adjustments. Analytically, teacher-level predictors are grand-mean centered and school-level aggregated predictors are group-mean centered to separate within- and between-school effects.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not use ILSA cognitive achievement outcomes with Plausible Values; instead, the dependent variables are teachers’ emotional exhaustion and job satisfaction measured via questionnaire scales. Because the outcomes are non-PV constructs, PV handling is not applicable by design. Missing data are addressed with full information maximum likelihood (FIML), which uses all available information under a missing-at-random assumption rather than PV-based combining rules.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Study 1: DiScH project in Schleswig-Holstein (northern German federal state). Schools were randomly selected within each school type; special needs schools were excluded, and only schools providing at least one teacher response for a relevant variable were included. Teachers participated voluntarily via an online survey (March–April 2021). The final analytic sample comprised 1022 teachers from 120 schools. Study 2: SchuMaS (Schule macht stark) program across Germany; 200 schools were surveyed and the final sample comprised 2886 teachers from 196 schools. Some questionnaire items were randomly assigned to reduce respondent burden, so analyses for occupational well-being and cooperation facets used only the available partial responses; missingness was assumed random and handled with FIML.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 the study leveraged Teacher age, Teacher gender, School type to predict predicted at the teacher level by health concerns (β≈0, finding that This paper is not an ILSA-based machine learning study; it analyzes two German teacher survey datasets (Study 1: DiScH, N=1022 teachers in 120 schools in Schleswig-Holstein; Study 2: SchuMaS, N=2886 teachers in 196 schools across Germany) to quantify between-school versus within-school variation in emotional exhaustion and job satisfaction. The authors use multilevel regression with random intercepts to separate teacher-level from school-level effects and report intraclass correlations (ICC(1), ICC(2)) and standardized regression coefficients (β). In Study 1, between-school variance in emotional exhaustion was low (ICC(1)=3.7%), while social interaction indicators showed substantial between-school variance (principals’ support ICC(1)=22.6%; cooperation ICC(1)=20.7%). Emotional exhaustion was predicted at the teacher level by health concerns (β≈0.29–0.34) and extra workload (β≈0.25–0.33), and negatively by principal support, cooperation, and digital competency. In Study 2, between-school variance in emotional exhaustion was higher (ICC(1)=9.9%), and school-level exchange was associated with lower exhaustion (β≈−0.99), while job satisfaction showed weaker school-level effects and more teacher-level associations with digital competency and professional collaboration. Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal inference) and reliance on self-reported measures aggregated to the school level. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse for ML-specific fields because the manuscript conducts multilevel regression analyses (random-intercept models) rather than training or evaluating machine learning algorithms. It also does not use ILSA/PISA/TIMSS/PIRLS-style achievement outcomes with Plausible Values; the dependent variables are questionnaire-based teacher well-being constructs. Therefore, ml_techniques, plausible-values handling, and PV-related performance metrics are not applicable to this study’s design.
